messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Marcus is a thirty-year-old carpenter who lives with his wife in a small town in the Pacific Northwest. He came to therapy at his wife’s insistence, though he was not sure what talking could do. He had not spoken about what happened in nearly two years, and he had come to believe that putting it into words was impossible anyway—the event existed somewhere in his body and his senses, not in language he could shape and share.

The trauma occurred on a job site. Marcus was framing a new house with a crew of five. A young apprentice named Derek was cutting a rafter on a table saw when the blade caught a knot in the wood. The piece kicked back and Derek’s hand slid into the blade. Marcus was ten feet away. He saw the blood spray across the plywood floor, heard the saw’s pitch change, saw Derek’s fingers separate and land. He remembered the sound—a wet, percussive thud—and the taste that rose in his own mouth: copper and sawdust, a metallic grit he could not swallow past. He had tried to help. He had grabbed a tourniquet from the first aid kit and wrapped Derek’s arm, but his hands were shaking and Derek was screaming and the blood kept coming. By the time the paramedics arrived, Marcus had stopped feeling his own body. He felt like he was watching the scene from somewhere above himself, a floating observer who could not move or speak.

In the months that followed, Marcus could not stop reliving it. The memory did not come as a story he could tell himself; it came as a full sensory assault, without warning. He would be reaching for a hammer and suddenly he would taste copper and sawdust again, and then he would be back on that plywood floor, the saw still whining, the blood still spreading. The reliving was so complete that he would lose track of where he actually was. He had learned to dissociate deliberately—when he felt the memory rising, he would try to blank out, to push himself outside his own body before the full force of it hit. He had come to believe that this was the only way to survive it.

He began to avoid thinking about the event at all. He would not let his mind go near it. If a coworker mentioned Derek’s name, Marcus would change the subject or walk away. He stopped eating lunch with the crew. He started eating alone in his truck, and then he started eating constantly—fast food, bags of chips, whatever he could get his hands on—because he had discovered that the fullness in his stomach could dull the edges of the flashbacks. He gained thirty pounds in six months. His wife noticed that he flinched when she touched his arm, and that he could no longer stand the smell of fresh-cut pine.

At work, he could no longer use a table saw. He would ask his foreman to assign him only framing or finishing work, anything that kept him away from the spinning blade. He told himself this was reasonable, that he was just being careful. But the avoidance had spread. He refused to go to the hardware store because the sawdust aisle triggered the taste. He stopped visiting his brother, who had a workshop in his garage. He told his wife he was tired, and he spent most evenings on the couch, eating and watching television, trying not to think.

Marcus had come to believe that his life was destroyed. He could not rely on himself anymore—he had frozen during the accident, and he was certain that if something happened again, he would fail again. He felt permanently damaged, changed in a way that could not be undone. He did not say this to anyone, but he thought it every day. He had stopped making plans for the future. He had stopped imagining a life that included children, or a house of his own, or a career that would last. He was just waiting.

What finally brought him to therapy was a single moment. He was driving home from a job site when a song came on the radio—a song that had been playing in Derek’s truck the morning of the accident. The taste returned. Marcus pulled over and vomited onto the shoulder of the road. He sat there for twenty minutes, shaking, unable to move. When he got home, his wife found him on the bathroom floor. He told her everything he could, which was not much. He said he did not know if he could keep going. She made the appointment the next day.

Marcus is afraid of what therapy will ask of him. He is afraid that putting the event into words will make it worse, that the words will not be enough and the memory will still come anyway. But he is also afraid of staying the way he is—permanently damaged, unreachable, eating himself into numbness on the couch. He does not know if he can change, but he is here, and that is more than he has done in two years.
